paragraphs.heading: Earth's scorching twin
paragraphs.text: Venus is the second planet from the Sun. It is so close to Earth in size and mass that it is often called Earth's sister or twin. Its diameter is 12,103.6 km, only 638.4 km short of Earth's, and it has 81.5% of Earth's mass. Yet Venus has no liquid water, and no other rocky body in the Solar System has an atmosphere nearly as thick and dense.

paragraphs.heading: A crushing greenhouse
paragraphs.text: The air is 96.5% carbon dioxide, with nitrogen making up most of the rest, and a thick layer of sulfuric acid clouds wraps the whole planet. All that carbon dioxide causes an intense greenhouse effect. At the surface the average temperature is 464 °C, the hottest of any planet, and the pressure is 92 times what we feel at sea level on Earth. Under those conditions the lowest layer of the atmosphere turns into a supercritical fluid.

paragraphs.heading: Slow and backward
paragraphs.text: Venus has no moons, and it turns very slowly in the retrograde, or backward, direction. This comes from a contest between the Sun's tidal pull and the uneven heating of its massive atmosphere. One Venusian day lasts 116.75 Earth days, about half of its 224.7-day year. Because it spins so slowly, Venus is very nearly a perfect sphere. Its magnetosphere is weak: with no internal dynamo, it is induced by the solar wind meeting the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A volcanic surface
paragraphs.text: Inside, Venus has a core, a mantle and a crust. The crust follows what is called stagnant lid tectonics: heat from inside escapes through active volcanoes, which resurface the planet from time to time. Smooth volcanic plains cover about 80% of the surface. The rest is two highland continents, Ishtar Terra in the north, about the size of Australia, and the bigger Aphrodite Terra just south of the equator, roughly as large as South America.

paragraphs.heading: Was Venus ever wet
paragraphs.text: Venus may have had liquid water and a habitable surface early on, until a runaway greenhouse effect evaporated it all. But studies of how gases break down in its present atmosphere suggest its volcanoes give off too little water to make oceans, so it has likely been hostile for its whole history. High up, at the level of the clouds, conditions are the most Earth-like anywhere in the Solar System. Possible signs of life reported there in 2020 sparked new research and missions.

paragraphs.heading: Watching and visiting
paragraphs.text: Through telescopes, Venus shows phases, and by 1613 these were offered as decisive evidence against the Earth-centered model and for the Sun-centered one. Venera 1 flew past Venus in 1961, the first interplanetary spaceflight. Mariner 2 returned the first data in 1962. Venera 4 reached the planet as the first impactor in 1967, Venera 7 landed in 1970, and Mariner 10 took the first images in 1974 while heading for Mercury.
